She declares that the PRC authorities are “following a very similar approach to what we have seen in the ROC” (p. 163), pointing to the emphasis on science planning, science education, and state and private sector coordination of R&D. While Greene rightly points out that a scientific renaissance is currently under way in the PRC, she argues with little conviction that policy makers in Beijing had much to learn from their Taiwanese counterparts. In fact, the PRC has looked to the experiences of Japan, South Korea, Europe, and the United States for more relevant insights than Taiwan. This is because the huge size and organizational structure of the Chinese economy and its S&T establishment is very different from its much smaller Taiwanese counterpart. While Taiwan may have some useful lessons in S&T development to offer, especially its horizontal linkages with the global technology order, they are likely to be of limited value for the PRC. Despite these limitations, this book overall helps to provide new insights into understanding the critical factors required for latecomer developmental states to successfully utilize S&T policy in their modernization efforts.

t: Fortifying China: The Struggle to Build a Modern Defense Economy – By Tai Ming Cheung
abs: Fortifying China: The Struggle to Build a Modern Defense Economy . Ithaca, NY : Cornell, NY University Press . xvi + 279 pages. ISBN 9780801446924 , $39.95 cloth . Cheung, Tai Ming . 2008 . It is well known that China's current level of development and growth hinges on reforms of the post-Mao period. In Fortifying China: The Struggle to Build a Modern Defense Economy, Tai Ming Cheung scrupulously explores this era of reform with regard to the defense economy. The book is a primer on the uneven rise of dual-use technology in China, given changes in the prioritization of innovation since the Chinese Communist Revolution. What is important and interesting to note is that there are political, bureaucratic, and technological fluctuations within the post-Mao era itself. Cheung is nevertheless optimistic that China is in a position to eventually catch up to the world's technology leaders given its institutions, entrepreneurialism, technology transfer, and relatively diminished role of the state. The first section of the text is a remarkable compilation and presentation of data and events from the Chinese Revolution to the present, to address the following questions: In the post-Cold War and reform eras, how has the Chinese defense economy dealt with limits to technological innovation? What strategies are used, spin-off and spin-off, in particular? Cheung begins with the preceding period—the Mao era (early/mid-1950s to the mid/late 1970s)—when the conventional defense sector and the strategic weapons sector ran on completely separate tracks. The former was slow, lacked input from scientists, lacked organizational incentives to innovate, and exhibited an institutionalized separation of R&D and production. Yet the strategic weapons sector was a great success because of its focus on linkages, R&D, and competence building. Downsizing of the defense economy in the wake of Deng's market liberalization and internationalization efforts was resisted by the military, which limited competition, entrepreneurship, and decentralization and ultimately hindered innovation and diffusion. How the central government dealt with fluctuations in levels of unemployment as a result of the conversion process is not addressed, though, when employees in defense-related work decreased from 3 million to 1–2 million. Similarly, from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, the authorities closed down enterprises operating at a loss. Other policies may have been designed to deal with these changes in employment, such as the Kejiao Xingguo (“revitalizing the country through science, technology and education”), but it is not confirmed. The defense industrial apparatus lagged behind the rest of the Chinese national innovation system (NIS) by the late 1990s, when Deng reprioritized the defense economy toward civilian and dual-use production, under national goals of economic development and a transformed bureaucracy. Increased exports and inward technological investment allowed the defense economy as a whole to gain access to advanced civilian technology and investment capital, modernize its organizational and management systems, and boost profits through exports. Cheung maintains that the defense economy's shift from duplicative imitation in the Mao era to creative imitation in the reform era was due to the application of the strategic sector's earlier successes to the entire industry. These efforts were bolstered as Zhu Rongji and Western-educated technocrats helped implement market reforms, including privatization of the state-owned sector and a diminished role of the state, particularly when granting concessions. With a simultaneous decline of power by the military bureaucrats, the late 1990s represented initial efforts to integrate the civilian and defense economies and forge reciprocating technology sharing between the military and civilian sectors. To deal with flaws of a corrupt institutional structure, the Four Mechanisms were implemented in 1998 to bolster competitiveness, oversight, and performance evaluations. Corrections to an otherwise weak system of intellectual property rights were made in this period to incentivize R&D, and competence building through the basic research efforts at Chinese universities was targeted. Still, China's quality of production in the defense economy is as much as two generations behind global standards, which Cheung attributes to insufficient capital investment, underdeveloped competitiveness, and innovation bottlenecks. Cheung then briefly compares the Chinese model with the United States and Japan, the world's two most innovative countries, and makes the following policy prescription: “create an economy with the civil-military technological synergies modeled on Japan but with a defense-industrial base on a scale comparable to that of the United States” (p. 233). To show how far China has come in this regard, Cheung looks at the Chinese space industry, notable for its successful antisatellite test but still plagued with innovation shortages. Cheung also calls for a revised, “semiopen” model of technological catch-up to deal with foreign restrictions on diffusion. This model emphasizes foreign investment and partnerships in the dual-use economy, but Cheung does not substantiate these prescriptions with even cursory data to show expected correlations between openness and growth of the defense sector. The sole theoretical structure referenced by Cheung is the NIS framework, addressing the most important activities and structures of China's innovation system: diffusion, learning processes, interactions between research organizations, absorptive capacity, and imitation. Secondary theories include international economics and international political economy, but they are undeservedly minimized in the book. Openness to foreign technology has been a stated goal for the Chinese defense economy since the late 1990s, and Cheung details the SU-27 fighter aircraft licensing agreement with Russia, which was ultimately coupled with indigenous efforts to generate the Shenyang J-11B fighter plane. The book's final pages, as well, address openness in light of a continuing “zero-sum” embargo of military arms and technology by the United States in the wake of the Tiananmen Square massacre. There are other theoretical absences in the book, particularly in terms of how diffusion might arise through an R&D collaboration framework. This would have been a welcome addition, as there is evidence of R&D collaboration throughout the book and as early as the Mao period, when a lack of organizational incentives to innovate was overcome by the creation of linkages between primary actors and counterparts associated with the conventional weapons system. Despite these concerns, Cheung is entirely correct in his call for more and multiple forms of innovation. The rich collection of primary, Chinese language-based sources and data had not been previously available in English. On these points alone, Fortifying China has valid applications for security, political economy and international political economy, and research policy specialists, and it is an excellent addition to existing discourse on the Chinese NIS.

t: Editors' Analysis: A Status Report of the Policy Studies Journal , 2004–09
Syllabi
The Evolution of the Theoretical Foundations of Punctuated Equilibrium Theory in Public Policy
abs: Punctuated equilibrium theory in public policy replicated from biological punctuated equilibrium theory has concluded that public policies alternate between stasis and punctuation. However, recent research on Pacific Northwest forest policy, U.S. state tobacco policy, and U.S federal auto efficiency policy have found no punctuations despite an attempt to do so. What is the efficacy of using biological punctuated equilibrium theory to also explain punctuated equilibrium in public policy? Significant differences exist between biological and public policy punctuated equilibrium theory including time frames for change, what constitutes outside disturbances of equilibrium, venues of punctuated equilibrium, levels of analysis for change, and patterns of change. Most policy research on punctuation has focused on the “tone” of media coverage related to change. Some recent studies concluding no punctuation occurred have focused on government action or inaction. Proving strong inference in scientific research requires a clear and viable syllogism linked to appropriate methodology. Both of these crucial elements are now in question in punctuated equilibrium research in public policy.

t: Technocracy, Politicization, and Noninvolvement: Politics of Expertise in the European Regulation of Chemicals
abs: This article addresses the relationship between scientific expertise and policy in European chemicals regulation. We argue that the role of scientific expertise in the European regulation of chemicals varies across decision‐making levels, countries, and stages of the policy process. Our case study of the role of scientific expertise in the regulation of brominated flame retardants illustrates considerably different manifestations of this interconnected process across regulatory arenas, even though this case concerns a single group of substances. On the European Union level, we find a mix of technocracy and politicization; in Sweden, a clear‐cut politicization; and in Poland, noninvolvement. Such differences can be explained by a combination of factors, in particular frame dominance, and mobilization of advocacy coalitions.

t: Policy Punctuations in Colorado Water Law: The Breakdown of a Monopoly
abs: The actors, influences, and processes that combine forces to change policy subsystems are modeled in punctuated equilibrium theory wherein monopolistic policy subsystems are broken down through changes in policy images and venue shopping spurred by a critical mobilization of actors. Studying a case of policy change in Colorado water rights, this research examines multiple levels of policy change—local, state, and cross‐case. This research finds that at the state level, punctuated equilibrium theory accurately explains the process by which policies changed to allow for recreational in‐channel uses of water. At the local level, however, these processes are not clearly evident. Using media coverage as a proxy measure for agenda status also shows that policy image change and high public agenda status did not lead to these policy changes within Colorado communities. This article discusses whether we should therefore discount punctuated equilibrium as a model of policy change in this case.

t: Patent Failure: How Judges, Bureaucrats, and Lawyers Put Innovators at Risk – By James Bessen and Michael J. Meurer
abs: Patent Failure: How Judges, Bureaucrats, and Lawyers Put Innovators at Risk . Princeton, NJ : Princeton University Press . 331 pages. ISBN 9780691134918 , $29.95 cloth . James Bessen and Michael J. Meurer . 2008 . This book's title leaves no doubt as to its main thesis—the patent system is not living up to its putative role, and rather than serving as a powerful provider of incentives for innovation, it has become a source of costs that, in most sectors of the economy, actually outweigh the benefits. The intellectual property rights that the system dispenses do provide private returns to their holders, “but taking the effect of other owners’ patents into account, including the risk of litigation, the average public firm outside the chemical and pharmaceutical industries would be better off if patents did not exist” (p. 16). The question asked is not whether property rights might be desirable for the intangible products of invention but whether patents in fact do work well as property. “The economic effectiveness of any property system depends not just on what it sets out to do, but also on the laws, regulations, institutions, and norms that implement the system . . . the messy details of how patents work matter” (pp. 7–8). The book's criticism of the patent system is organized around the notion of the “notice” function of property, i.e., the ability of the system to notify non-owners of property boundaries. Such a function is problematic for patents because of the intangible nature of the underlying assets. The failure of patents to provide clear notice as to the scope of the claimed property inevitably exposes inventors to costly disputes and litigations. The central empirical aim of the book is to determine how such costs compare to the benefits that patents confer to their owners. To assess the (private) value of patents, the book presents the results of two main approaches. One relies on patent renewal behavior. Because owners must pay a fee at regular intervals to keep a patent valid, a decision not to renew indicates that the holder values the patent in question at less than the preset renewal fee. Data on renewal decisions are therefore informative as to the distribution of patent values, and, given some ancillary assumptions, one can calculate the average value of a patent (and thus the value of the populations of patents). The other method of valuing patents, which can be used for public firms, relies on the study of the firms’ market value vis-à-vis their assets and patents portfolio. The expected cost of patent litigation is teased out from data on how the stock price of public firms reacts to the news of patent lawsuit filings. The authors find that apart from the chemical and pharmaceutical industries, the expected cost of disputes and litigations has considerably exceeded the total imputed value of patents (to the firms themselves) since the mid-1990s. On the whole, therefore, for most industries the patent system is proving to be a tax for innovators rather than an incentive. The remainder of the book provides an interpretation of the increasing cost of litigation that started in the 1990s, discusses the role of patents for small inventors, and, by focusing on the proliferation of patents for abstract claims, makes a comprehensive case for the negative impact of software patents. The authors argue that to be effective, patent reform must address the problem of patent notice squarely by making patent claims more transparent and restricting vague language and overly abstract claims. Other proposed changes include increasing patent fees and tightening the non-obviousness standard to stem the flood of patents and promoting deference by the Federal Circuit to the Patent Office on matters of claim interpretation. This is an ambitious book. It marshals an impressive array of evidence, ranging from sophisticated empirical economics to the actual workings of legal institutions, to support a striking conclusion: except for the chemical and pharmaceutical industries, the U.S. patent system might actually be an obstacle to innovation. The analysis is tantalizing, but just how convincing is it? One of its avowed principles is to eschew lofty theorizing in favor of a careful empirical construction. Perhaps a tighter theoretical framework would help clarify matters. Conclusions such as “reform should push the patent system toward the real property system by making patent claims more similar to the boundary of land” (p. 239) betray an unresolved ambivalence about the nature of intellectual property rights. That these rights must be distinctive, one might argue, is precisely because standard property rights, which typically work well for “private goods,” are ill-suited to deal with the “public good” nature of the products of inventive activities, the private value of which can be easily destroyed by the free riding of imitators. As for what the data themselves can tell us, as many an economist knows, clear and convincing empirical results are rare. Take, for example, the estimation of patent values based on patent renewals, which plays a critical role in the book's findings. About 40 percent of patents are renewed to full term, and for these patents all we know is that the owners value them more than the few thousands of dollars it takes to renew. That is, renewal data have virtually nothing to say about the value of the most valuable patents! This points to a fundamental identification problem, which the book (and others) solves by assumption, by invoking a specific distribution of patent values (e.g., the lognormal). Similar concerns can be raised about the other empirical methodologies used in the book to value the private benefits and costs of patents. That might be the best one can do with patent data, but it still raises the question of whether it is enough to support the authors’ draconian conclusions. The book adds to a growing number of dissatisfied voices concerned with the poor performance of the U.S. patent system. The topic is timely, as the Patent Reform Act of 2009, working its way through Congress at the time of this writing, grapples with some of the very issues analyzed in the book. The originality of Bessen and Meurer's approach, and the weight and detail of the evidence they provide, makes the book most worthwhile reading for anyone interested in how institutions and policies can foster innovation in a market economy.

t: Integration of Environmental Concerns in a Trans ‐Atlantic Perspective: The Case of Renewable Electricity
abs: The issue of integrating environmental concerns into energy policy decision making is increasingly addressed, not least related to climate change. Although the United States, unlike the EU, did not sign the Kyoto Protocol, several U.S. states promote renewable electricity (RES‐E), and some of these initiatives are linked to climate‐change mitigation efforts. The present article assesses in this connection the six New England states of the United States, comparing their efforts of integrating RES‐E with climate change to the Nordic countries in Europe. In order to explain different approaches, the article focuses on the importance of different EU and U.S. multilevel governing structures. The analysis indicates that the New England states' RES‐E promotion thus far has not been substantially integrated with climate‐change concerns, whereas in the EU's more top‐down approach, climate change figures more prominently vis‐à‐vis RES‐E. EU policies represent an increasingly important driver for the Nordic countries. In the United States, on the other hand, it remains an open question as to how future federal policy efforts will relate to existing policies at the state level.

abs: Scholars of Chinese politics, political economy, and modern history should find this book a useful addition to existing scholarship on China's fourth-generation leadership.This book also provides insights for those studying China's economic modernization.The final chapter notes the difficulty much of the technocratic leadership has in adapting to the market economy.It may be that China's innovation and technological strengths and weaknesses have arisen in part because of the training of their leaders as engineers and not as entrepreneurs.However, it is also in this chapter that Andreas arguably misinterprets the challenges faced by the Red Engineers and their progeny in the new economy.Rather than weakening the hold of China's existing technocratic class, reform may instead have strengthened their control.China's richest citizens are the heirs of political leaders.Political capital has transferred itself into economic capital.It may be that cultural power is declining in importance relative to political and economic, but in many cases there remains a fair degree of overlap.While the current technocratic class is likely to become less technocratic over time and more business and economic capital oriented, the membership will remain largely the same.Nonetheless, as Andreas notes, Tsinghua will remain at the top of this structure, training the next generation of China's leaders.

t: Syllabi
The Limits and Opportunities of Networks: Municipalities and Canadian Climate Change Policy
abs: Research on climate change policy and politics has become increasingly focused on the actions and influence of subnational governments. In North America, this attention has been particularly focused on why subnational governments have taken action in the absence of national leadership, what effect action might have on future national climate policy, and whether the collective action of networks of municipal governments are reshaping and challenging the character of national and global climate governance. This paper examines Canadian municipal climate in light of the absence of a comprehensive and effective climate national strategy. The paper considers various reasons why local governments in Canada have not been central players in national plans, and why their actions have not been more influential nationally. The paper argues that the potential influence of Canadian municipalities on national climate policy is weak, given the loose nature of the network and the long‐held structural view that municipalities are not significant units of political analysis in national political and policy debates. The paper concludes by considering the constraints and opportunities of subnational climate networks and municipal network analysis.

t: Public Opinion, Risk Assessment, and Biotechnology: Lessons from Attitudes toward Genetically Modified Foods in the European Union
abs: Proponents of biotechnology argue that citizens' opposition to innovations such as genetically modified (GM) foods is rooted in emotionalism, media and nongovernmental organizations' distortions of good science, and scientific ignorance. Critics charge that this “risk management discursive” is too reductionist, exaggerates scientific capacity, inappropriately privileges scientific values over social and political values, and inaccurately captures how citizens evaluate biotechnology. This article uses ordered logit analysis applied to the responses of Europeans to a 2005 Eurobarometer survey to test the validity of these competing perspectives in the area of GM foods. Our analysis supports the arguments of those calling for the inclusion of broader discursive social, political, and cultural elements in deliberations over GM foods. Analysis also shows that citizens are less emotional in evaluating GM foods than proponents claim and supports this “new politics of knowledge” perspective, but citizens also cling more tightly to hopes that science can resolve debates with objective analysis.

t: Justice for All? A Cross‐Time Analysis of Toxics Release Inventory Facility Location
abs: This paper contributes to the environmental justice literature by addressing several outstanding issues in a single study. Using a cross‐time data set that allows us to control for the prevalent “chicken‐and‐egg” or “which‐came‐first” problem, we analyze the relative importance of poverty and race/ethnicity in an analysis that includes economic costs, potential legal costs, and potential collective action. Because the most appropriate functional form is not obvious, we use several methods, including Tobit, Poisson, and ordinary least squares, on different forms of the dependent variable. In every case, controlling for the population present at the time of disamenity location and controlling the other factors mentioned, we find evidence of disproportionate collocation based on race/ethnicity, but not on poverty alone. We also find that the potential for collective action decreases the likelihood of receipt of the studied disamenities.

t: Public Lands Policy and Economic Trends in Gateway Communities
abs: From the mid‐1960s through 1980, major policy changes were adopted as a result of federal and state public lands protection statutes. This article analyzes the impact these policy changes have had upon the economies of gateway communities, a subject of limited discussion in the scholarly literature. One conclusion is that gateway community economies have become less dependent on resources extraction. This analysis finds that several factors––beyond policy change––have influenced the shift away from resources extraction. Likewise, there is the question over what economic mainstays have stepped in to fill the resources extraction void? For many gateway communities, it appears that the answer has been recreational tourism. The implications of this economic shift within gateway communities are explored.

t: Railway Dreaming: Lessons for Economic Regulators from Aboriginal Resource Management Lore
abs: Railway reform in the past decade has seen the introduction of mandated third party access to track in a number of jurisdictions. This article argues that third party access changes the property rights associated with railway track, rendering it a common pool resource. As such, it is useful to ask whether the literature on the governance of common pool resources could inform the economic regulation of railways. This article suggests that it might, and draws some lessons from the common pool resource governance mechanisms traditionally used by Australia's Aborigines in managing their land that may have application within the context of the railways.

t: Technological Empowerment: The Internet, State, and Society in China – By Yongnian Zheng
abs: If you only have time to read one book about the Internet in China, this succinct and readable book would be a good choice.If you are interested in the Internet, then you should read about China, as China is now the country with the most Internet users.Author Yongnian Zheng does not radically reshape our understanding, but he does contribute important arguments at the leading edge of this burgeoning field.Early studies of the Internet in China confidently predicted that it would undermine the Party's authoritarian rule.A second wave of scholarship documented that Chinese authorities had promoted rather than obstructed the Internet and had controlled its uses.Professor Zheng acknowledges the Party's effective management of the Internet but argues that the Internet strengthens both state and society and leads to their mutual transformation and toward political liberalization.The introductory chapter succinctly reviews vast swathes of literature.Zheng recounts how Chinese have debated science and democracy over the last hundred years.He explains that Chinese elites have adopted science as a means of strengthening the state, and links this to theorists such as Michel Foucault, Lawrence Lessig, and James Boyle, who have shown how code, surveillance, and so forth can be used to strengthen the state's control over society.The second chapter applies this theme to the present by showing how contemporary Chinese leaders have adopted "neotechnonationalism" and promote the Internet as primary means of strengthening and legitimating their rule.Zheng's third chapter makes it difficult to argue that his relatively optimistic conclusions are based on any failure to recognize the full extent of repression.It ends with a nine-page appendix listing all of those reported arrested for Internet offenses.There are also extensive charts and tables listing government organs responsible for managing the Internet and the laws and regulations they enforce.Readers may be able to find more on the technologies used by Chinese censors in Berkman Center publications.A very few recent developments such as the "fifty cent party" of seemingly ordinary Internet users who are secretly compensated for posting pro-government remarks evidently came to light too late to be included.Nonetheless, this is a very competent account of the structure and intent of China's formidable system of Internet regulation.In alternate sections in the first two chapters and in the fourth chapter, Zheng advances a parallel argument showing how the Internet empowers society.Using "state and society" as an analytic foundation will strike some China scholars as a distorting simplification, but Zheng repeatedly emphasizes that both state and society need to be disaggregated and t: An Experimental Study of Opinion on Climate Change: Labile Causalities and Stable Realities
The Next Catastrophe: Reducing Our Vulnerabilities to Natural, Industrial, and Terrorist Disasters – By Charles Perrow
abs: The Next Catastrophe: Reducing Our Vulnerabilities to Natural, Industrial, and Terrorist Disasters . Princeton, NJ : Princeton University Press . vii +377 pages. ISBN 9780691129976 , $29.95 cloth. ISBN 978140082759 , $29.95 e-book . Perrow, Charles . 2007 . Much-respected, oft-quoted sociologist and organization theorist Charles Perrow uses this book to broadly update, revise, and expand his seminal 1984 (re-released in 1999) book, Normal Accidents: Living with High-Risk Technologies. In nine well-researched and engaging chapters, Next Catastrophe also makes many worthy and insightful contributions to the study of disasters and disaster management organizations. Perrow cogently illuminates the perils of human dependence on tightly coupled, interactively complex, difficult to control, under-regulated, and vulnerable technologies—particularly technologies whose failures are capable of producing massive negative consequences. Perrow explains socio-technical and political phenomena concerning disasters and disaster vulnerabilities in a very convincing and clear way. He is able to capture and retain his reader's interest through well-documented vignettes and storytelling. He advances his theories and uses them to explain and interpret events that have transpired in recent years. In Next Catastrophe, Perrow advocates smarter ways to reduce systemic organizational vulnerability to natural disasters and human-caused disasters, within the latter terrorism particularly. Perrow posits that there are three general causes of disaster: natural causes, organizational causes, and deliberate causes. His elucidation of failure categories—executive failure, mundane organizational failure, technological failure, regulatory failure—is excellent. He maintains that because of how we are organized to approach them, terrorism, industrial accidents, and natural disaster forces are likely to become worse and produce more damage; for Perrow the threat of catastrophe is growing, not diminishing. In Chapters 3 and 4, Perrow offers a short history of the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and a thoughtful account of the 9/11 disaster. There is a critical review of the George W. Bush administration's treatment of federal emergency management after 9/11 and well into the Department of Homeland Security years from to 2003 to 2006, and a scathing description of the failures of emergency management before, during, and after the Hurricane Katrina catastrophe of 2005. Perrow generally lavishes praise upon, and withholds criticism of, the Clinton administration's FEMA (led for almost eight years by James Lee Witt), although Perrow is less forgiving when it comes to the Clinton administration's terrorism attack preparedness and prevention policies. Perrow anticipated the current policy dispute over whether FEMA should remain part of the Department of Homeland Security or be set free as theindependent agency it was from 1979 to 2003. He favors FEMA's liberation but avoids a full discussion of the political, intergovernmental, and budgetary consequences of such a policy decision. This is a minor quibble given how well and how often Perrow integrates his governmental and political commentary into his chapters and arguments. In Chapters 5 through 7, Perrow revisits some of his stock-in-trade technology categories. He gives us new and updated insight into the commercial nuclear power, chemical, and electric utility industries. He shows that a variety of disaster events occurring in each of these realms since 1984 have both confirmed his original thesis and made evident that many officials in government and the private sector have yet to heed his original (now 25-year-old) warnings and lessons. Chapter 8 concerns terrorism on the Internet. It parallels and extends points from Perrow's chapter on the national electric power grid: Chapter 7. A theme carried through almost all chapters concerning physical infrastructure is the need for deconcentration. Perrow criticizes the heavy dependence on Microsoft operating systems and underestimation of the threat posed by hackers, yet he describes with awe the decentralized, always evolving, and resilient design of the Internet itself. In other chapters, he asserts that dispersion and downsizing of critical industrial facilities, particularly facilities whose substances and processes pose a major health or environmental threat to plant workers and nearby communities, should be an essential strategy to mitigate and prepare for the eventualities of terrorism, the forces of nature, and accidents or malfunctions. This is easier said than done. In the United States, the “ ‘not in my backyard’ syndrome,” the very much warranted environmental justice movement, and perhaps foremost, environmental impact statement requirements at the federal and state levels, all combine to confound attempts to “deconcentrate” dangerous industrial facilities to many new and more remote locations. With the major exception of the Bhopal chemical disaster in India, Perrow does not much explore corporate out-sourcing of dangerous facilities from developed nations to developing nations. Perrow has corollary arguments beyond deconcentration. Building redundancy into important systems is both logical and wise. Networked systems carry many benefits but they also embody unpredicted dangers as well. Decentralization is better than fragmentation. Deregulation has combined with the avarice of corporate capitalists, especially whose firms use dangerous substances or critical technologies, to increase vulnerabilities. Government's failure to formulate and implement effective regulation is blamed for a host of economic and technical debacles. Perrow offers many examples of the deficiencies and abuses of schemes that rely on “self-regulation” or voluntary compliance. This work enhances Perrow's reputation as a premier scholar of socio-technical organization studies. Some may be mildly disappointed that Perrow has not used Next Catastrophe to present a completely new set of profound theories. However, through this work he has refined, perfected, and extended his “normal accident” and system-behavior theories. He offers enlightenment about the causes and effects of the catastrophic and disastrous events of the last quarter century. He has generated important lessons and prescriptions for avoiding or mitigating calamities or possible catastrophes of the future. This book will join and perhaps lead a burgeoning literature on catastrophe. This book should be required reading for emergency management and homeland security workforces. Perrow facilely assembles a solid body of factual information drawn from original documents, interviews, and secondary sources while he simultaneously advances his own narrative. The Next Catastrophe will long stand as a major contribution appreciated by scholars and students of both technology policy and disaster policy.
